summary: Improves XMPP security in two ways: it establishes a strong association between a domain name and an XML stream through prooftypes, and it explains how to securely delegate a service domain name to a target server host.

plainLanguage.summary: A chat server proves which name it belongs to and who it is working for.

questions: what is xmpp domain name association
how to delegate an xmpp domain securely
what is a prooftype in xmpp
how does xmpp server dialback work
subtitle: How XMPP proves a server really owns its domain name, and how to delegate that name safely to a host.

tldr.problem: XMPP clients and servers must verify that the server they reach really is the domain they asked for, but certificates are hard to get and deploy when one server hosts many domains.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC introduces prooftypes, mechanisms that tie a domain name to an XML stream, and describes three: PKIX, DANE and POSH. It also explains secure delegation of a service domain name to a hosting server.
tldr.outcome: Operators can pick the prooftype that fits their setup, since DANE needs secure DNS and POSH needs a web server with a CA certificate. Future prooftypes must fit the same model.

today: RFC 7712 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update. Its POSH prooftype is defined in RFC 7711.

sections.title: Why Domain Name Associations Matter
sections.content:
In XMPP, a client or peer server needs a strong association between the DNS domain name of a service (such as example.com) and the XML stream it opens with that service. In other words, it must verify the identity of the server it connects to, and servers must verify incoming connections from other servers.

RFC 6120 assumed this Domain Name Association (DNA) would be proved with the PKIX prooftype: the server presents a PKIX certificate, and the client's verification material is a trusted root obtained out of band. This RFC generalizes that model so other prooftypes can be defined, provides a basis for modernizing them as DNS Security matures, describes the flow of operations, and gives guidelines for secure delegation of a service domain name to a target server hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: When you call a number, you want to be sure it really is your friend and not someone pretending. Chat servers need to check names in the same way.

sections.title: Client-to-Server Flow
sections.content:
The client-to-server case is simpler because the client does not assert a domain name, so verification only goes one way. The simplified order of events is:

  1. The client resolves _xmpp-client._tcp.a.example via DNS.
  2. It opens a TCP connection to the resolved address.
  3. It sends a stream header addressed to='a.example'.
  4. The server answers with a stream header saying it is a.example.
  5. TLS negotiation takes place, and the server presents a PKIX certificate.
  6. The client checks the certificate against the XMPP profile of the RFC 6125 matching rules and RFC 5280. If it passes, the client accepts the association.

The certificate might not be acceptable, for example because the server hosts several domains, or because it is self-signed. A self-signed certificate means the client must use a fallback process or ask the user to accept an unauthenticated connection.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock, the server says its name, and it shows an ID card. You check that the card matches the name you were looking for.

sections.title: Server-to-Server Flow and Its Wrinkles
sections.content:
The server-to-server case is more complex because associations are checked in both directions. In the simple case Server 1 (a.example) connects to Server 2 (b.example). They exchange stream headers, Server 2 presents a certificate and asks for one, and Server 1 presents its own. Each checks the other's certificate, which gives mutual authentication. Once one direction is established, SASL EXTERNAL can establish the other.

The RFC lists the assumptions behind this happy path: both certificates are acceptable, no extra domains are involved, administrators can get certificates from a widely accepted CA, and they run their own servers.

When Server 2 does not accept Server 1's certificate, it falls back to Server Dialback (specified in XEP-0220). Server 1 sends a db:result with a dialback key. Server 2 connects back to a.example and sends a db:verify with the key. Server 1 replies with type='valid', and Server 2 can then establish the association.

Piggybacking lets one connection carry more domain pairs. In assertion, a server hosting c.example as well as b.example sends a db:result for the new domain over the existing stream. In supposition, a server offers to reuse a connection for a sub-domain such as rooms.a.example when the existing certificate is also valid for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two servers have to check each other, like two people swapping ID cards. If one card looks odd, they can call back on the number they already know to confirm, and one phone call can cover several names.

sections.title: The Three Prooftypes: PKIX, DANE and POSH
sections.content:
Sometimes administrators cannot or will not get valid PKIX certificates for every domain. A CA might email an address the sub-service administrator cannot read, a host may not want to hold a tenant's private key, or managing so many certificates is too much work. Two alternatives to PKIX are described.

DANE: the proof is a service certificate or domain-issued certificate. The client gets its verification material through secure DNS (see RFC 7673), which is needed so that a chain of trust runs from the certificate to the DNS root. If there is no SRV record, the fallback methods of RFC 6120 apply.

POSH: the proof is a PKIX certificate. The client gets a hash of it over HTTPS at a well-known URI, as defined in RFC 7711. Secure DNS is not necessary because the HTTPS fetch relies on the PKI's chain of trust. The URIs are /.well-known/posh/xmpp-client.json for client-to-server and /.well-known/posh/xmpp-server.json for server-to-server.

For both, the domain name of the TLS client's reference identifier comes from the to address of the initial stream header, because TLS SNI is purely discretionary in XMPP.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to show an ID: a card from an official office, a record in the phone book, or a note on the owner's own web page.

sections.title: Prooftype Model and Secure Delegation
sections.content:
A prooftype is a mechanism for proving an association between a domain name and an XML stream. It defines the nature of the server's proof, the matching rules, how the client obtains its verification material, and whether it depends on secure DNS. PKIX, DANE and POSH all fit. Other prooftypes are possible, such as TLS with PGP keys, Kerberos or OAuth tokens, or Server Dialback keys, but this RFC does not define a Dialback prooftype.

Multi-tenancy is a common way to run XMPP. For example, an SRV record can delegate example.com to hosting.example.net. Without DNSSEC, delegation by SRV record is inherently insecure. In practice, large hosts end up with either unencrypted server-to-server traffic or TLS where certificates are not checked. End users are forced to override warnings or pin certificates for the host's name. RFC 7673 gives secure delegation for DANE using DNSSEC, and RFC 7711 gives it for POSH using HTTPS redirects.
sections.plainLanguage: A prooftype is a recipe for showing proof. Handing your name over to a landlord is only safe if someone can check that you really agreed to it.

sections.title: Guidance for Server Operators
sections.content:
What an operator must do depends on the prooftypes it supports.

  • PKIX: get certificates for the XMPP server from a CA. DNS Security is not required.
  • DANE: the operator can generate its own certificates or get them from a CA. DNS Security is required.
  • POSH: certificates can be self-generated or from a CA, but a web server for the POSH files with a CA certificate is also needed. DNS Security is not required.

These burdens add up when several prooftypes are supported. The RFC calls that unavoidable if domain name associations are to succeed in the largest possible percentage of cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of ID needs its own paperwork. If you want to accept all of them, you do all the paperwork.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
For the PKIX prooftype this document supplements but does not supersede the security considerations of RFC 6120 and RFC 6125. For DANE and POSH the reader is sent to RFC 7673 and RFC 7711. Any future prooftype must thoroughly describe how it conforms to the prooftype model.

IANA considerations are small: this RFC registers two POSH service names, xmpp-client and xmpp-server, in the registry created by RFC 7711.
sections.plainLanguage: Each way of showing an ID has its own safety rules, and this paper points to them rather than repeating them.
